content.p: For about a week in October 1937, the army of the Dominican Republic killed ethnic Haitians and Dominicans of Haitian descent along the country's northwestern frontier. The historian Richard Turits, of the University of Michigan, puts the toll at an estimated 15,000 people killed by machete between 2 and 8 October. Other writers give higher or lower figures, and Hyperallergic notes that there is no official record of the number. The dictator who ordered it, Rafael Trujillo, was never punished, according to Paulino, and Turits writes that his regime turned the scandal into a founding moment for an anti-Haitian nationalism rather than a crime to be answered for.

The event is now most often called the Parsley Massacre, after the claim that soldiers tested victims by making them pronounce the Spanish word for parsley, perejil. In Haiti it is remembered as Kout Kouto, the knife blow. In the Dominican Republic the older names were El Corte, the cutting, and El Desalojo, the eviction.
content.h2: A border that had been fluid
content.p: Turits describes a frontier where, before 1937, Haitians and Dominicans, most of them independent peasants, lived side by side. The border was fairly open and carried no immigration restrictions. Strikingly, he writes, the official line since Trujillo took power in 1930 had been more friendly to Haiti than hostile to it, so the massacre "seemed to come out of nowhere". He adds that Haitian workers in the cane fields, which lay elsewhere, were with few exceptions not targeted.

Edward Paulino, a historian at John Jay College and a co-founder of the Border of Lights group, traces Trujillo's interest in the frontier back to 1930. The region had long been a route for runaway slaves, smugglers and insurgents, and it lay beyond the reach of the elites in Santo Domingo. Paulino argues that the dictator had to wait for several conditions. He first had to eliminate his rivals at home. He also needed the departure of American forces from Haiti in 1934, which until then had checked his power, and he had to settle the long-disputed boundary line. A Haitian-Dominican commission surveyed the frontier, Trujillo and Haiti's president, Sténio Vincent, negotiated, and both countries signed definitive border treaties in 1935. By 1937, Paulino writes, the two governments were enjoying a diplomatic honeymoon.

Trujillo himself came from a working-class family in San Cristóbal. Paulino notes that his maternal grandmother was Haitian and that he rose through the National Guard, which American forces had created during their occupation of the Dominican Republic from 1916 to 1924.

On 2 October 1937, in the border town of Dajabón, Trujillo made a speech that Paulino quotes: "And we have already begun to remedy the situation. Three hundred Haitians are now dead in [the town of] Bánica. This remedy will continue."

Drawing on diplomatic correspondence and oral histories, Paulino says the operation ran for several weeks and was planned a year or more beforehand. People who were Black and judged to be Haitian, whether men, women or children, were arrested, taken to secluded places in the countryside and murdered, mostly with machetes. In his account, the choice of weapon was meant to avoid the appearance of a premeditated, large-scale army operation. At the Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library he found a diplomatic message from the American ambassador, R. Henry Norweb, who called the killings "a systematic campaign of extermination".

The Haitian Times, reporting in 2024, describes soldiers armed with machetes, pregnant women beheaded, children's skulls crushed and bodies thrown into the river that divides the two countries, which Haitians have called Rivyè Masak, Massacre River, since the 1700s. Its dating is slightly wider than others: late September into early October.

The test that gave the event its popular name was linguistic. Haitians speak Kreyol, in which the letter r is softer, and a Spanish word such as perejil was used as a shibboleth. Paulino cautions that the test was often beside the point. Many of the people targeted were bicultural and bilingual Dominican-Haitians, and, as he puts it, it did not matter to their killers. He interviewed both survivors and perpetrators, as did the scholars Lauren Derby and Richard Turits and the journalist Juan Manuel García before him.

Latino USA, working on a radio special for the 80th anniversary, interviewed Francisco Pierre, then 90, mostly blind, and living in Ouanaminthe, just inside Haiti. He said he was born in 1927 in Loma de Cabrera, and was ten at the time of the killings. On 5 October 1937, he recalled, a Haitian man passing the house shouted to his uncle that they must cross into Haiti at once because people were being killed in the village.

The family went up past the cemetery, and he said they could hear the cries from the village. His grandmother loaded a donkey and carried a pot of fried meat on her head. Along the way they met a blind man, and later walked with a woman who knew him. On a path near a crossroads they were stopped by two young Dominicans on a mule and a horse. Pierre said that one of them, who had once been treated for illness by the woman travelling with them, would not kill her. When the group reached the water that marks the border, he said, they saw a number of dead bodies, and Haitians on the far bank called to them to hurry because soldiers were coming. They were helped across, and the soldiers arrived just after.

Afterwards, as Latino USA reports, the Dominican government claimed it had nothing to do with the killings, which it presented as an uprising by local Dominican farmers against Haitian thieves. Paulino describes the same account, in which patriotic farmers were defending their land from Haitian cattle rustlers. Hyperallergic adds that until Trujillo was assassinated in 1961 the massacre was officially regarded as an isolated farmers' revolt. Latino USA says that for more than twenty years nobody could investigate what had happened while Trujillo was in power, and that researchers began travelling to the border to interview survivors only afterwards.
Paulino says that no single reason explains Trujillo's decision, and he sets out several views while saying, "We will never know. There is no smoking gun."

One view holds that, by clearing the border of Black Haitians, Trujillo sought to whiten the nation, in a policy known as blanqueamiento. Paulino notes the contradiction: the government kept importing thousands of Haitians to cut sugarcane. A second view stresses the Great Depression, with Trujillo wanting to secure and colonise the borderland as an agricultural export base. A third, held by others, is that the massacre aimed at unseating Vincent, whose government sheltered anti-Trujillo exiles, and replacing him with pro-Trujillo officials. A fourth is that Trujillo saw himself as a modern Napoleon and eventually meant to invade Haiti.

Paulino also points to an unusual feature. In most mass killings the ideological campaign comes first, preparing society for violence against a targeted group. Here, he writes, citing Turits and Derby, the violence came first and a state doctrine of anti-Haitianism followed.

Turits says the Dominican government feared armed retaliation and temporarily moved women and children out of the border areas. Haiti's military did nothing to defend or avenge its people. At first President Vincent banned public discussion of the killings and refused to let the church hold masses for the dead. On 15 October, Haiti and the Dominican Republic jointly issued a statement hoping that "certain incidents" on the northern frontier would not be the subject of "exaggerated commentary", and declaring that relations had not been damaged.

Pressure grew inside Haiti. There were demonstrations and strikes, and in December a coup attempt failed. Vincent eventually demanded an international investigation and mediation. Trujillo would not accept an inquiry and offered an indemnity instead. Turits says one can only speculate why Vincent accepted $750,000, of which only $525,000 was ever paid, in exchange for ending the arbitration. Hyperallergic says the sum followed an American investigation. The agreement, signed in Washington on 31 January 1938, stated that the Dominican government recognised "no responsibility whatsoever" for the killings. The Haitian Times says that the 1938 agreement worked out to a "paltry" $37 per survivor, and that none of them ever received it.

Trujillo used the occasion to defend himself. In a statement to the governments that witnessed the agreement, Mexico, Cuba and the United States, he said it was more than an indemnity because it set new laws to restrict migration between the two countries, and he spoke of the "worst Haitian element". Turits reads this as the regime defending the massacre as a response to a mythical illegal immigration, and turning a scandal that might have toppled it into the founding moment of an anti-Haitian nationalism.

In November 1937 Trujillo opened a criminal investigation into the "incidents" on the frontier. By March, according to Turits, it had produced convictions of dozens of Dominican civilians who were obliged to confess to killing 423 Haitians. He says neither those trials nor the agreement with Haiti ended the terror: in spring 1938 Trujillo ordered a new campaign against "Haitians" in the southern frontier, during which thousands were forced to flee and hundreds were killed.

Among Dominicans in the northern frontier, Turits writes, communities lost roughly half their populations to killing or flight and found a closed border where movement had been free. Some saw the massacre as an inexplicable horror. Others, above all their children, took up the old anti-Haitianism of urban elites and came to believe the killings had restored the frontier's true Dominican character.

Paulino writes that neither Trujillo nor any senior official was ever punished, that no truth commission was ever formed, and that after the dictatorship ended in 1961 the Dominican Republic elected Joaquín Balaguer, one of Trujillo's highest-ranking officials, as president. The government meanwhile pursued what Paulino calls the Dominicanization of the border, settling colonists from the interior and building institutions in the region.

Paulino links the massacre to a 2013 Constitutional Tribunal decision, Ruling 168-13, which withheld citizenship from people born to undocumented residents and, he writes, fell hardest on long-settled Haitian residents and their Dominican-born children. A later law, 169-14, was meant to soften its effects. In his words, Haitians were excluded from the border by the knife in 1937 and today are excluded from the nation by the judicial pen.

The authors Julia Alvarez and Edwidge Danticat said on NPR in 2012 that the history had been met with enormous silence. Alvarez grew up not knowing about it, and Danticat said it was not something discussed but was transmitted through history. Alvarez tied it to the present, saying that the "massacre mentality" persists in the denial of the rights of Haitians and Dominicans of Haitian origin.

In the absence of official commemoration, Paulino writes, the Border of Lights collective has held annual events on the border since 2012. It holds a candlelight vigil from Dajabón to the border checkpoint, and an online vigil in which people send in photographs of themselves holding candles. Paulino says the idea was first proposed by Alvarez and Michele Wucker, and that the vigil is perhaps the only time victims receive such a public acknowledgment.

The living memory is thinning. In 2024, The Haitian Times spent five days with ten survivors in the Ouanaminthe area, in towns such as Dosmont and Ferrier. One of them, Marcellus Jean, died aged 102 between interviews, and his family said financial reparations might have eased his last days. The survivors and their families see compensation as a matter of dignity as well as money, and one survivor, Joseph, told the paper: "We have waited too long." She asked: "Where is our justice?"

The event also reached film. The feature film Parsley, directed by José María Cabral, closes with the caption "No international court dealt with the 'Parsley' Genocide." Hyperallergic's reviewer called the film's violence a difficult watch and set the toll at 4,000 to 20,000.
